title: A fossil in the making
caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 201, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: HCG 7, NGC 201 · constellation Cetus · about 200 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Hubble shows NGC 201 in fine detail, with a bright centre and barred spiral arms. The arms do not start directly at the core but seem offset, growing from a bar of stars that cuts through the middle. Like the Milky Way, it is a barred spiral. It lies 200 million light-years away in Cetus, the Sea Monster, and cannot be seen with the naked eye.

NGC 201 and three close neighbours outside the frame make up HCG 7, one of the Hickson Compact Groups. These are small, isolated gatherings of a few bright, compact galaxies close together. As they draw nearer, they interact strongly, pulling material into space and distorting one another.
Eventually, all the galaxies in such a group will merge. Simulations show that within a billion years they combine into one giant fossil galaxy, and this may be the final fate of all galaxy groups.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.02 x 2.83 arcminutes) and distance (200 million light years), the frame spans roughly 176,000 × 165,000 light-years. Its light set out about 200 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and combines visible and near-infrared filters. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: NGC 201 is invisible to the naked eye, and part of this image is near-infrared light, which the eye cannot detect.

explore: William Herschel discovered NGC 201 in the late 1700s. A version of this image was submitted to Hubble's Hidden Treasures competition by Luca Limatola.
alt: A barred spiral galaxy with a bright centre and spiral arms growing from a bar across its middle.
